description: The lives and teachings of the prophets Nuh, Ibrahim, Ismail and Yusuf as told in the Qur'an.
content_html:
The Prophets in Islam

In Islam, Allah has sent a series of prophets to guide humanity. All share the same core message: submit to Allah, worship him alone, and live justly. Each prophet faces opposition, suffers for his message, and ultimately depends on Allah rather than human approval. The Qur’an’s prophet stories are not simply biographical — they are theological templates for how every believer should respond to Allah’s call.

The Prophet Nuh (Noah)

Nuh is one of the earliest prophets in Islamic tradition. He is described in Surah 17:3 as a “grateful servant” (shakur) — his defining characteristic is thankfulness to Allah even when his mission was almost entirely rejected. Surah 71 (Nuh) is devoted entirely to his story. He preached to his people for 950 years (a figurative number expressing the duration of his mission). He called them day and night, publicly and privately, offering them forgiveness if they would turn to Allah.

They refused. They mocked him. They blocked their ears and put their fingers in them so as not to hear. Only a small group believed. Allah then commanded Nuh to build the Ark. The flood came, destroying the rest — including Nuh’s own son, who refused to board the ark and drowned. This detail is unique to the Qur’anic account: Nuh’s son is separated from him by his disbelief, and Allah tells Nuh that the son is not “of your family” because his actions were not righteous. Faith, not biology, defines the community of Allah.

After the flood, Nuh is told to disembark with “peace and blessing from us on you and on some of the peoples who will descend from you.” His significance as a messenger is confirmed in Surah 17:3: he is “a grateful servant” — a description that, in the Qur’an, connects thankfulness (shukr) with faith. To be ungrateful is a form of denial of Allah; to be grateful is a form of worship.

The Prophet Ibrahim (Abraham)

Ibrahim is the most important of the earlier prophets in Islam. He is described in Surah 37:109–111 as receiving Allah’s “peace and salutations” because he proved faithful, and as one who “tended always towards good deeds.” He is known as Khalilullah — the “Friend of Allah.”

Ibrahim’s story involves multiple tests. He was raised in a community of idol-worshippers — including his own father, who made idols. Ibrahim recognised the absurdity of worshipping created objects and challenged his community. In Surah 21:57–58, he is described as destroying the idols of his people, leaving only the largest standing so that people would have to ask “who did this?” — a dramatic act designed to make people think critically about what they were worshipping.

With his wife Hajra (Hajra) and son Ismail, Ibrahim established the sacred site of Makkah. In Surah 2:127–129, Ibrahim and Ismail together raise the foundations of the Ka’ba and pray: “Our Lord, accept this service from us… Our Lord, make us Muslims submitting to you, and of our descendants a Muslim nation submitting to you.” The prayer is answered in the community of Islam itself.

Ibrahim is also commanded to sacrifice his son. The Qur’an does not name which son in the sacrifice narrative itself (Surah 37:99–111). Most Muslim scholars traditionally identify the son as Ismail rather than Isaac (as in Genesis 22), based on the context of the narrative which places Ibrahim in the land of Makkah with Ismail. However, some Muslim scholars across history have argued it was Isaac, following the identification of the earlier revelation in the Tawrat. The debate is acknowledged in the spec. At the moment of sacrifice, Allah intervenes and ransoms the son with a great sacrifice — both are spared. This event is commemorated annually in Id-ul-Adha.

Key Fact

The Qur’an does not name the son in Ibrahim’s sacrifice (Surah 37). Most Muslim scholars traditionally identify him as Ismail based on context (Ibrahim is in Makkah with Ismail when this happens). Some scholars, however, have argued it was Isaac. The spec notes this as a “possible debate” — students should know both positions without asserting that the Qur’an definitively says one or the other.

The Prophet Ismail

Ismail is mentioned in Surah 21:5–86 among the earlier prophets. His characteristics as described in the Qur’an include patience and perseverance. He is also described as obedient to his parents and as commanding his family to pray and give zakah. In the Ka’ba-building narrative (Surah 2:127–129), he works alongside his father, symbolising both physical labour in service of Allah and the passing of faith from one generation to the next.

Ismail’s place in the prophetic chain is significant: Islamic tradition holds that Muhammad descended from Ismail through the Arab line, fulfilling the prayer Ibrahim and Ismail made when building the Ka’ba: “Send among them a messenger from among them.” Ismail thus links the story of Ibrahim to the coming of the Prophet Muhammad.

Key Fact

Nuh’s defining virtue is shukr (gratitude), shown in Surah 17:3. Ibrahim’s Ka’ba prayer (Surah 2:127–129) explicitly asks Allah to “send among them a messenger from among them” — Muslims understand this fulfilled in Muhammad. The son in the sacrifice (Surah 37) is unnamed; most classical Muslim scholars identify him as Ismail, but the debate exists and examiners award marks for acknowledging it.

The Prophet Yusuf (Joseph)

Yusuf’s story is told in Surah 12 — the only surah of the Qur’an devoted entirely to one prophet’s life. The opening verse calls it “the best of stories.” The narrative is rich with human emotion: jealousy, betrayal, temptation, imprisonment, patience, forgiveness and reunion.

Yusuf has the gift of dream interpretation. His brothers, jealous of their father’s love for him, throw him into a well and lie to their father Jacob, telling him Yusuf was eaten by a wolf. Yusuf is found by a passing caravan and taken to Egypt where he is bought as a slave. He is wrongly accused and imprisoned, but his faith and patience sustain him. In prison he interprets the dreams of fellow prisoners correctly.

Pharaoh has a dream that no one can interpret. Yusuf’s ability is remembered, and he interprets it: seven years of plenty followed by seven years of famine. Pharaoh releases and honours him, placing him in charge of Egypt’s food stores. The famine brings his brothers to Egypt seeking food. After a series of tests, Yusuf reveals himself and forgives them: “No reproach on you this day; Allah forgives you, and He is the Most Merciful of those who show mercy.”

Each prophet embodies a virtue that Muslims are called to imitate. Nuh: perseverance and gratitude despite near-total rejection. Ibrahim: courage, rational faith and total submission to Allah even when it costs everything. Ismail: patient obedience across generations. Yusuf: moral integrity under pressure, patience in suffering, and generous forgiveness of those who wronged him. The Qur’an repeatedly draws explicit lessons from these stories for the current reader, using the phrase “in this is a sign for those who reflect.”

The prophet stories also emphasise that prophets were human beings, not divine. They suffered, they wept, they were tested. This is important for Islamic theology: the prophets are honoured and their example is followed, but they are not worshipped. Only Allah is worthy of worship (Tawhid). Venerating a prophet to the point of directing worship to them would itself be a form of shirk.

Many of the Qur’anic prophet stories have parallels in the Hebrew Bible and the New Testament. Muslims believe the Qur’an is the final, uncorrupted revelation — where the Bible’s version differs, the Qur’an provides the authoritative account. The key differences in these four prophets include: Nuh’s son who dies (not in Genesis); Ibrahim’s idol-smashing (not in Genesis); the identification of the sacrifice son as Ismail (Genesis says Isaac); Yusuf’s moral emphasis on forgiveness and gratitude to Allah (which echoes the Genesis narrative very closely — one of the clearest instances of the Torah being confirmed by the Qur’an). Muslims use the term Tawrat for the Torah, acknowledging it as an earlier divine revelation while affirming that the Qur’an is the final, preserved revelation.
exam_tip_html: This lesson covers four prophets — know the surah reference for each: Nuh (Surah 71), Ibrahim (Surah 37:109–111; 2:127–129; 21:57–58), Ismail (Surah 21:5–86; 2:127–129), Yusuf (Surah 12). For the 5-mark source question, citing the surah earns the mark: “In Surah 2:127–129, Ibrahim and Ismail together build the Ka’ba…” For questions on the sacrifice, acknowledge the debate: most Muslim scholars say Ismail, but the Qur’an does not name him — this nuance earns marks at the top level. SPaG: use the Islamic names (Nuh, Ibrahim, Ismail, Yusuf) not the biblical names (Noah, Abraham, Ishmael, Joseph) when answering on the Qur’an — but you can mention the biblical name in brackets to show your knowledge of both traditions.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Nuh (Surah 71) is the prophet of perseverance and gratitude; his son’s death by drowning shows that faith, not family, defines the community of believers.
  • Ibrahim (Surah 37; 2:127–129) is ‘Friend of Allah’ who builds the Ka’ba with Ismail; his sacrifice command is central to Id-ul-Adha — most Muslim scholars identify the son as Ismail, though the Qur’an does not name him.
  • Yusuf (Surah 12) — the only surah wholly devoted to one prophet — tells ‘the best of stories’: dreams, betrayal, prison, patience and ultimate forgiveness model the Muslim virtues of trust in Allah and generosity towards enemies.

practice_questions.text: Outline three things that Surah 71 (Nuh) teaches about the Prophet Nuh.
practice_questions.marks:
One mark per discrete point:
• Nuh preached to his people for a very long time, calling them day and night, publicly and privately — showing great perseverance in the face of repeated rejection.
• His people refused to listen, mocking him and blocking their ears — only a small group believed.
• Allah commanded Nuh to build the Ark; after the flood he was called a 'grateful servant' (shakur) in Surah 17:3.

practice_questions.text: Describe what the Qur'an says about Ibrahim and Ismail building the Ka'ba (Surah 2:127-129).
practice_questions.marks:
One mark per point:
• Ibrahim and Ismail together raised the foundations of the Ka'ba in Makkah.
• They prayed: 'Our Lord, accept this service from us' — asking Allah to receive their act of worship.
• They prayed for their descendants to be a Muslim community and asked Allah to 'send among them a messenger' — a prayer Muslims see as fulfilled in the Prophet Muhammad.

practice_questions.text: Explain two ways in which the story of the Prophet Yusuf (Surah 12) is important for Muslims today.
practice_questions.marks:
Two marks per point:
• Yusuf's patience through betrayal, slavery and imprisonment shows that trusting Allah even in extreme suffering brings ultimate vindication — his story encourages Muslims to maintain faith and integrity when life is unjust.
• Yusuf's forgiveness of his brothers ('No reproach on you this day; Allah forgives you') models Islamic values of forgiveness and reconciliation, showing that forgiving those who have wronged you is a sign of closeness to Allah.

practice_questions.text:
Explain two ways in which the story of Ibrahim in the Qur'an shows what it means to submit to Allah.
In your answer, refer to a source of wisdom and authority.
practice_questions.marks:
Two marks per point plus one for named source:
• Ibrahim's destruction of the idols (Surah 21:57-58) shows that submission to Allah requires rejection of all false gods — even when his own community and family worshipped them, he acted on his rational recognition that created objects cannot be divine.
• Ibrahim's willingness to sacrifice his son (Surah 37:99-111) represents the ultimate test of submission — he placed obedience to Allah above even his natural love for his child; the intervention of Allah (providing an animal instead) confirmed that his submission was accepted.
The fifth mark requires citing Surah 21:57-58 or Surah 37:109-111 as the named source.

practice_questions.text:
'The story of Ibrahim is the most important prophet story in the Qur'an.'
Discuss this statement.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (10-12): Both sides developed with named sources; justified conclusion.
Secure (7-9): Both sides present; at least one source.
Developing (4-6): One side stronger; few sources.
Emerging (1-3): Minimal.

In support: Ibrahim is described as 'Friend of Allah' (Khalilullah) — a unique honour. He is the ancestor of the Prophet Muhammad through Ismail. He built the Ka'ba — Islam's most sacred site. His willingness to sacrifice his son is commemorated in Id-ul-Adha, one of the two great Muslim festivals. He is the model of rational faith that rejects idolatry.
Against: Surah 12 calls Yusuf's story 'the best of stories' — suggesting it has a unique quality of narrative depth and moral richness. Nuh is described in Surah 17:3 as a 'grateful servant' — a profound model of perseverance. Muhammad is described as the Seal of the Prophets and is the one who received the final, complete revelation — in that sense the most important. Non-religious observers might question the entire concept of prophetic authority, arguing that moral wisdom does not need to be divinely authorised.

practice_questions.text: Outline three ways in which the Prophet Nuh's story is similar to or different from the Bible's account of Noah.
practice_questions.marks:
One mark per point (similarity or difference):
• Both the Qur'an and the Bible describe Nuh/Noah building an ark at God's command to survive a flood — the basic structure of the story is shared.
• In the Qur'an (unlike Genesis), Nuh's own son drowns in the flood because he refuses to believe — this detail is unique to the Qur'anic account.
• Both accounts describe Nuh/Noah as a righteous man chosen by God for his faithfulness in a corrupt generation.

knowledge_checks.q: Which surah is entirely devoted to the story of the Prophet Nuh?
Surah 12 is called 'the best of stories' and is devoted entirely to which prophet?
Ibrahim and _____ together raised the foundations of the Ka'ba in Makkah (Surah 2:127-129).
The Qur'an describes Nuh as a 'grateful servant' (shakur) in Surah _____ :3.
Match each prophet to their key story element:
right: Built the Ark and survived the flood; son drowned
Destroyed his people's idols and built the Ka'ba
Sold into slavery in Egypt; interpreted Pharaoh's dreams

flashcard_questions.q: What is Nuh described as in Surah 17:3?
flashcard_questions.a: A 'grateful servant' (shakur) — his thankfulness to Allah is his defining characteristic.

flashcard_questions.q: Which surah is entirely devoted to Nuh?
What happened to Nuh's son in the Qur'anic account that doesn't appear in the Bible?
flashcard_questions.a: He drowned in the flood because he refused to believe — showing faith, not family, defines the community.

flashcard_questions.q: What is Ibrahim called in Islamic tradition?
What did Ibrahim and Ismail build together (Surah 2:127-129)?
flashcard_questions.a: The Ka'ba — the most sacred site in Islam, in Makkah.

flashcard_questions.q: Does the Qur'an name the son Ibrahim was commanded to sacrifice?
flashcard_questions.a: No — it does not name him; most Muslim scholars traditionally identify him as Ismail, not Isaac.

flashcard_questions.q: What is Surah 12 and what makes it unique?
flashcard_questions.a: Surah Yusuf — the only surah devoted entirely to one prophet's story; called 'the best of stories'.

flashcard_questions.q: What special ability did Yusuf have?
flashcard_questions.a: Interpreting dreams — used to advise Pharaoh about seven years of plenty and seven of famine.

flashcard_questions.q: How does Yusuf respond when he reveals himself to the brothers who betrayed him?
flashcard_questions.a: 'No reproach on you this day; Allah forgives you, and He is the Most Merciful.'

flashcard_questions.q: What is the Tawrat and how does it relate to the prophet stories?
flashcard_questions.a: The Torah — the earlier divine revelation to Moses; Muslims see Qur'anic accounts as confirming or correcting the Tawrat.

glossary_terms.definition: Prophets and messengers sent by Allah throughout history to guide humanity; Islam recognises 25 named in the Qur'an and many more unnamed.
The prophet known as Noah in the Bible; called by Allah to warn his people, he built an ark to survive the flood; described as thankful (shakur) to Allah in Surah 17:3.
The prophet known as Abraham in the Bible; called 'the Friend of Allah' (Khalilullah), he is the ancestor of both Arabs and Jews and is central to Islamic faith.
Hagar in the Bible — the mother of Ismail; left by Ibrahim in the desert of Makkah, her desperate search for water is commemorated in the Hajj ritual of Sa'y.
The cubic black-clothed structure at the centre of the Masjid al-Haram in Makkah, considered the most sacred site in Islam; Muslims face it in prayer.
The prophet known as Ishmael in the Bible; the son of Ibrahim and Hajra, who helped build the Ka'ba and whose descendants include the Prophet Muhammad.
The prophet known as Joseph in the Bible; the subject of Surah 12 (Yusuf), the only Qur'anic surah devoted entirely to one prophet's story.
Yusuf's God-given ability to interpret the meaning of dreams; central to his story in Surah 12 and the means by which he rises from prison to power.
